h1: The 8 Best Ultrawide Monitors Under $500 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 ultrawide monitors under $500, all 3440x1440, compared on refresh rate, USB-C, curve and stand for work and gaming.
summary: The Dell S3425DW is the best ultrawide under $500: USB-C with 65W power, 95% DCI-P3 and up to 120Hz. The LG 34WR55QK-B is the productivity pick, and the AOC CU34G4V is the best gaming value at 180Hz. Console and mixed-GPU players have better fits in the Alienware and MSI.
intro: Every monitor here shares the same bones: a 34-inch curved VA panel at 3440x1440. That sameness is useful, because it strips the decision down to what really separates them. One USB-C cable that charges your laptop, a refresh rate that matches your graphics card, how tight the curve bends a spreadsheet and whether the stand can raise a screen this tall.

We compared the spec sheets for eight ultrawides under $500 and ranked them by how many buyers each would suit. Productivity features count heavily, since most people buy an ultrawide for work first and play second. Gaming-first models sit lower, though several of them are excellent at it, and a few cost a lot less than the leaders, which makes the ranking closer than the scores suggest.

products.name: Dell 34 Plus USB-C Curved Monitor (S3425DW)
products.verdict: USB-C with 65W power, 95% DCI-P3 color and a fast panel make it the best all-rounder.
products.description:
The Dell S3425DW is a 34 inch 3440x1440 curved VA monitor with refresh up to 120Hz, a listed 0.03ms response, USB-C with 65W Power Delivery, 99% sRGB and 95% DCI-P3. One cable carries video and charges a thin laptop, which clears the desk of power bricks. Color coverage at this level also makes it usable for light photo work.

It ranks first because no rival here combines USB-C and wide color with fast refresh. The LG offers USB-C too but tops out at 100Hz, while the AOC reaches 180Hz and has none.

Buy it if you work on a laptop and also game. The caveat is refresh: 120Hz is below the 180Hz of most rivals, and the stand is basic, so you may want a VESA arm.
products.skipIf: You want the highest refresh rate.

products.name: LG 34WR55QK-B
products.verdict: USB-C 65W, Reader Mode and picture-by-picture make it a desk-work specialist.
products.description:
The LG 34WR55QK-B is a 34 inch 3440x1440 curved VA monitor at 100Hz, with USB-C 65W power delivery, Reader Mode, picture-by-picture, OnScreen Control software and a height and tilt stand. Reader Mode is tuned for long documents, and picture-by-picture shows two sources side by side.

It ranks second because it is an office tool first. It matches the Dell on USB-C power and beats it on stand adjustment, but trails on refresh and color coverage, and gaming is not its aim.

Buy it if you spend your day in documents and spreadsheets on a laptop. Skip it if you play fast shooters. It has fewer ports than the gaming models, so check your peripheral count against the back panel before you order.

products.name: AOC CU34G4V
products.verdict: 180Hz, 0.5ms MPRT and a stand that raises 130mm, at a price well under $300.
products.description:
The AOC CU34G4V uses a 1500R curve on a 34 inch 3440x1440 VA panel running at 180Hz with a 0.5ms MPRT response, FreeSync Premium and a stand that adjusts for height, swivel and tilt, with a 130mm height range. A 1500R curve is gentle enough for spreadsheets, and the stand rises where cheap monitors do not.

It ranks third since it has no USB-C, so laptop users need a separate charger, and its color coverage trails the Dell. It does cost well under $300 and beats the MSI on response.

Buy it if you game on a desktop and want an adjustable stand. Skip it if you dock a laptop over USB-C. Pair it with a graphics card that can drive 3440x1440 near 180 frames, or the refresh rate is wasted.
products.idealFor: Gamers who want an adjustable stand.
products.skipIf: You dock a laptop with USB-C.

products.name: MSI MAG 346CQ
products.verdict: Certified for G-Sync Compatible and FreeSync, with 180Hz, 3000:1 contrast and a height stand.
products.description:
The MSI MAG 346CQ is a 34 inch 3440x1440 curved VA monitor running at 180Hz with a 1ms MPRT response, 3000:1 contrast, G-Sync Compatible and FreeSync certification, a height-adjustable stand and built-in speakers. Dual sync certification is useful if you swap between NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards over its life.

It ranks fourth because response is slower than the AOC's 0.5ms and it also lacks USB-C. The 3000:1 contrast gives deeper blacks than the Dell, but the speakers are basic.

Buy it if you might switch GPU brands and want sync to work either way. Skip it if you want a USB-C laptop dock. Treat the speakers as a backup, since a desk with a headset or external speakers will sound better.
products.idealFor: Gamers who may switch GPU brands.
products.skipIf: You want a USB-C laptop dock.

products.name: Alienware AW3425DWM
products.verdict: 180Hz, 1ms response and a console mode, backed by a 3-year warranty.
products.description:
The Alienware AW3425DWM is a 1500R 34 inch VA monitor at 180Hz with 1ms response, 3000:1 contrast, a dedicated console mode and a 3-year warranty. Console mode matters because most consoles do not output true 21:9, so a dedicated setting helps manage the picture.

It ranks fifth because it costs more than rivals with similar specs, such as the AOC, and lacks USB-C. The 3-year warranty is longer than the Dell's Premium Panel coverage, and an advantage over the AOC.

Buy it if you play on both PC and console. Skip it if you want a USB-C dock. Gaming styling is loud, so consider the look on a work desk too. Check the console's output modes, as black bars are typical.
cons: Costs more than rivals with similar specs
products.idealFor: Players who use PC and console.

products.name: ASUS TUF Gaming VG34VQ3B
products.verdict: Four USB 3.2 ports, built-in speakers and a 3-year warranty on a 180Hz panel.
products.description:
The ASUS TUF Gaming VG34VQ3B is a 1500R 34 inch VA monitor at 180Hz with four USB 3.2 ports, built-in speakers, 90% DCI-P3 and a 3-year warranty. Four downstream USB ports let you plug a keyboard, mouse, headset and drive into the monitor instead of the tower.

It ranks sixth because it lacks USB-C power delivery and the stand is less flexible than the AOC's 130mm height range. It does offer more USB ports than any rival here.

Buy it for a desk crowded with wired peripherals. Skip it if you dock a laptop over USB-C. The speakers are modest, and 90% DCI-P3 trails the Dell's 95%, so color work is not its strength.
products.skipIf: You dock a laptop over USB-C.

products.name: Samsung 34" Odyssey G5
products.verdict: The tightest curve here, at 1000R, with 165Hz, HDR10 and FreeSync Premium.
products.description:
The Samsung Odyssey G5 has a 1000R curve on a 34 inch 3440x1440 VA panel at 165Hz with HDR10 and FreeSync Premium. A 1000R curve is the tightest here, and it wraps the screen around your view, which adds immersion in single-player games.

It ranks seventh because the curve distorts straight lines in documents and design work, and it lacks USB-C. At 165Hz it also trails the 180Hz rivals.

Buy it for immersive single-player gaming where the wrap is the point. Skip it if you do design or spreadsheet work, because straight lines bend noticeably toward the edges. A 1500R screen such as the AOC is easier to live with in the office.
products.skipIf: You do design or spreadsheet work.

products.name: SANSUI 34" Curved UWQHD Monitor
products.verdict: The least expensive way into 3440x1440, with 200Hz, 97% DCI-P3 and HDMI 2.1 ports.
products.description:
The SANSUI 34 inch curved monitor is a 3440x1440 VA panel running at 200Hz, with 97% DCI-P3, PiP and PbP modes, two HDMI 2.1 ports and DisplayPort 1.4. The 200Hz figure is the highest here, and 97% DCI-P3 beats the Dell on paper.

It ranks last because the brand is less known, stand details are thin and no USB-C is listed. The warranty is also weaker than the Alienware's or ASUS's three years.

Buy it for a tight budget with a PC to feed it. Skip it if you want the strongest warranty. Use the return window to judge the stand and panel before you commit to a long-term setup.
products.idealFor: Tight budgets with a PC to feed it.

methodology.title: Productivity features
methodology.description: USB-C power delivery, picture-by-picture and reading modes carried weight, since most ultrawides are used for work first.

methodology.title: Refresh and response
methodology.description: Refresh rate and listed response time were scored against what a 34-inch VA panel can deliver in games.

methodology.title: Color coverage
methodology.description: sRGB and DCI-P3 figures show which monitors suit photo and video work as well as gaming.

methodology.title: Stand and ergonomics
methodology.description: Height adjustment matters on a wide screen, so stand range counted toward each ranking.

methodology.title: Value within the field
methodology.description: Features and warranty were compared against price bracket relative to the others here.

whatMatters.detail: A USB-C port with 65W Power Delivery carries video and charges a laptop through one cable. It is only worth paying for if you use a laptop, since without it you need a separate charger and video cable. Check the wattage on the listing and compare it with your laptop charger, because lower numbers will not charge a larger laptop under load.

whatMatters.factor: Curve radius is a comfort choice
whatMatters.detail: A 1000R curve is tighter than 1500R, so the screen wraps more around you. Tighter feels more immersive in games but can bend straight lines in documents. Most work-focused buyers are happier with 1500R or gentler curves. The Samsung Odyssey G5 uses 1000R, while the AOC, Alienware and ASUS use 1500R.

Going from 60Hz to 100Hz or 120Hz is obvious. From 120Hz to 180Hz, the difference is smaller and mostly matters for fast shooters. Check that your graphics card can drive 3440x1440 at those rates before you pay for them, because a card that manages 90 frames wastes a 200Hz panel, and the upgrade then buys you nothing.

whatMatters.factor: VA panels trade angle for contrast
whatMatters.detail: All eight monitors use VA panels, which have deeper blacks and higher contrast ratios than IPS but narrower viewing angles. Sit directly in front of the middle of the screen and the sides stay readable. Do not plan on a very close seat or on sharing the screen with someone beside you, as color shifts at the sides.

whatMatters.factor: Stand height matters on a wide screen
whatMatters.detail: A 34 inch ultrawide is tall as well as wide, so a fixed low stand can leave the top edge too high or too low. Look for a listed height range such as the AOC's 130mm. If the stand is fixed or thin on details, check that the back has a VESA pattern so you can fit an arm instead, and confirm the arm's weight rating.

howToChoose.intro: Decide what the monitor will do most.

cards.label: USB-C docking
cards.text: One cable carries video and 65W to a laptop. Picks: Dell S3425DW and LG 34WR55QK-B.

cards.label: Gaming speed
cards.text: Higher refresh and faster response, but no laptop charging. Picks: AOC CU34G4V, MSI MAG 346CQ, Alienware AW3425DWM, ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B, SANSUI.

howToChoose.note: Choose USB-C if you use a laptop daily. Choose speed if your PC does the work.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Enough USB ports for a keyboard, mouse and drives, and a stand that does not eat desk depth.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B, which lists four USB 3.2 ports and built-in speakers to cut desk clutter.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use a laptop daily or edit photos. The Dell S3425DW's USB-C and color coverage justify the premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You game on a desktop PC. The AOC CU34G4V or SANSUI already deliver 180Hz or more.

faq.q: Is 3440x1440 good enough, or do I need 4K ultrawide?
faq.a: For a 34 inch screen, 3440x1440 is a sharp, practical resolution and far easier on a graphics card than 4K. All eight monitors here use it, so the choice comes down to refresh, USB-C and stand design.

faq.q: Do I need a USB-C monitor?
faq.a: Only if you use a laptop. The Dell S3425DW and LG 34WR55QK-B offer 65W power and video over one cable. For a desktop PC, USB-C adds little, and the AOC or MSI deliver faster refresh for less.

faq.q: Is a curved ultrawide good for work?
faq.a: Yes, especially at 1500R or gentler. The curve keeps the edges within view. The Samsung's tighter 1000R curve suits games better than documents, where straight lines can appear to bend near the edges.

faq.q: What refresh rate do I need?
faq.a: For office work, 100Hz is plenty. For gaming, 144Hz to 180Hz feels very smooth. Check that your graphics card can drive 3440x1440 at that rate before paying for the AOC, MSI or SANSUI.
Many consoles do not output true 21:9, so they show black bars. The Alienware AW3425DWM has a console mode designed for this case. Check what your console outputs before choosing any ultrawide.

faq.q: Can I mount these on a monitor arm?
faq.a: Many monitors support VESA mounts, but ultrawides are heavy and wide. Check the listing for VESA support and the weight limit of your arm before you buy. A fixed stand makes an arm especially useful.

finalTake: The Dell S3425DW is the right ultrawide under $500 for most buyers, because USB-C, strong color and a quick panel suit both work and play. The LG fits office-first users, and the AOC CU34G4V is the gaming bargain. Decide on USB-C and refresh rate first, since the resolution is the same on all eight.
